## Effect of Accessibility on Active Travel
The marginal-effect curves show how the predicted percentage of active travel changes across the range of each accessibility measure, with all other covariates held at their average. Because the spline coefficients are not directly interpretable, these curves give a clearer picture of each measure's effect on the response scale. Figure 17 shows the two curves. The two measures entered their models on different scales (the kriging measure on its original scale and the walking measure on a log10 scale), so the curves should be read individually rather than compared by their position on the horizontal axis. They can, however, be compared on the vertical axis, since both predict the same outcome.
The kriging curve (left) is gentle and slightly non-monotonic. Predicted active travel changes only modestly across the range of kriged density, moving within a band of roughly 41% to 44%, and the credible interval is wide. This indicates that kriged school-place density has only a small and uncertain association with active travel once demographic differences are accounted for.

The walking curve (right) is much steeper and has a clear S-shape. Predicted active travel rises from around 15% at the lowest levels of walking accessibility to around 60% at the highest, and the credible interval is narrow throughout. This indicates a strong and fairly certain association: areas where more school places can actually be reached on foot have substantially higher active travel.

Comparing the two curves on the vertical axis, the walking measure is associated with a much larger change in active travel than the kriging measure, and with greater certainty. This is consistent with the severance pattern described earlier: what matters for active travel is not simply how close schools are in straight-line terms, but whether they can actually be reached on foot. The walking measure captures this directly, which may explain why it is more strongly associated with active travel than the straight-line kriging measure.

```{r marginal-effects-both, echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, fig.width=12, fig.height=6, out.width="100%", fig.cap="Marginal effect of each accessibility measure on predicted active-travel percentage, with other covariates held at their average. Left: kriged density (original scale). Right: walking accessibility (log10 scale). The curves should be read individually, not compared by horizontal position."}

library(brms); library(tidyverse); library(patchwork); library(splines)

model_urban_krig <- readRDS("D:/Final-Project/model/models/model_urban_krig_splines.rds")
model_urban_walk <- readRDS("D:/Final-Project/model/models/model_urban_walk.rds")
df_urban_model   <- readRDS("D:/Final-Project/model/data2/df_urban_model.rds")

# helper: hold all numeric predictors at their mean, vary one column
make_newdata <- function(df, vary_col, grid) {
  template <- df %>% summarise(across(where(is.numeric), ~ mean(.x, na.rm = TRUE)))
  nd <- template[rep(1, length(grid)), ]
  nd[[vary_col]] <- grid
  nd$prop_weight <- 1
  nd
}

# kriging
kg <- seq(quantile(df_urban_model$krig_value_per_100_3_18, .01, na.rm=TRUE),
          quantile(df_urban_model$krig_value_per_100_3_18, .99, na.rm=TRUE), length.out=100)
ndk <- make_newdata(df_urban_model, "krig_value_per_100_3_18", kg)
pk  <- fitted(model_urban_krig, newdata = ndk, scale="response", probs=c(.025,.975))
plot_krig <- bind_cols(ndk, as_tibble(pk)) %>%
  mutate(across(c(Estimate,Q2.5,Q97.5), ~.x*100))

# walking
wg <- seq(quantile(df_urban_model$log10_walk_30, .01, na.rm=TRUE),
          quantile(df_urban_model$log10_walk_30, .99, na.rm=TRUE), length.out=100)
ndw <- make_newdata(df_urban_model, "log10_walk_30", wg)
pw  <- fitted(model_urban_walk, newdata = ndw, scale="response", probs=c(.025,.975))
plot_walk <- bind_cols(ndw, as_tibble(pw)) %>%
  mutate(across(c(Estimate,Q2.5,Q97.5), ~.x*100))

# kriging on its own (linear) scale
p_krig <- ggplot(plot_krig, aes(krig_value_per_100_3_18, Estimate)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin=Q2.5, ymax=Q97.5), alpha=.2) + geom_line(linewidth=1) +
  labs(title="Kriging accessibility effect",
       x="Kriged school-place density (per 100 children)",
       y="Predicted active travel (%)") +
  theme_minimal() + theme(plot.title=element_text(face="bold"))

# walking on its log10 scale
p_walk <- ggplot(plot_walk, aes(log10_walk_30, Estimate)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin=Q2.5, ymax=Q97.5), alpha=.2) + geom_line(linewidth=1) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks=c(0,1,2,3,4),
                     labels=c("1","10","100","1,000","10,000")) +
  labs(title="Walking accessibility effect",
       x="Walking accessibility (per 100 children, log scale)",
       y="Predicted active travel (%)") +
  theme_minimal() + theme(plot.title=element_text(face="bold"))

p_krig + p_walk
```

# Discussion

## Interpretation of Results
The central finding of this study is that how schools are reached matters more than how close they are in straight-line terms. The two accessibility measures agreed on average but diverged in many individual CSAs, and the areas where they diverged most pointed consistently to severance, where physical barriers such as motorways, rivers, and water separate an area from schools that are nearby as the crow flies. This interpretation is supported by the statistical model. The walking accessibility measure, which is based on actual network travel time, had a strong and fairly certain association with active travel, while the kriged density measure, which is based on straight-line distance, had only a small and uncertain association. Taken together, the comparison and the model suggest that straight-line measures of school-place availability can overstate how reachable schools really are, and that network-based measures capture the practical opportunity for active travel more faithfully.

These findings connect back to the "postcode lottery" idea that motivated the study. They suggest that unequal opportunities for active school travel are not only about where schools are located, but also about whether the local network allows children to reach them on foot. Two areas with similar straight-line access to schools can have very different walking opportunities if one is cut off by a barrier. This points to the potential importance of local 
infrastructure, such as pedestrian crossings and routes across or around barriers, as well as the broader distribution of school places, in shaping opportunities for active school travel.

## Limitations
A number of limitations should be kept in mind when interpreting these results. The outcome data are restricted by the way school travel information is released in official statistics. The Census data provide aggregated travel-to-education counts for Census Small Areas, rather than individual-level journeys between home and school. As a result, the analysis cannot observe the actual school attended by each pupil, the exact route taken, or whether pupils travel to primary or post-primary schools. The model therefore estimates area-level associations between school accessibility and active travel, rather than individual travel behaviour, and the results should be interpreted as evidence of spatial association, not as proof that improved accessibility directly causes higher walking or cycling rates.

The active-travel outcome is also not separated by school type. Primary and post-primary pupils may have different travel distances and school-choice patterns: younger children may depend on nearby primary schools, while older students may travel further to fewer, more specialised post-primary schools. Because the Census outcome combines both groups, the analysis cannot distinguish these patterns. Future work could repeat the analysis separately for primary and post-primary schools where the data allow, although this may be limited by the availability of travel-mode outcomes disaggregated by school type at fine spatial scales.

The school accessibility measures use enrolment as a proxy for school places. Enrolment provides a consistent measure of the relative size and spatial distribution of schools, but it does not measure spare capacity, catchment areas, admissions policies, or whether a place is realistically available to a child living in a particular area. This limitation is especially relevant where schools are oversubscribed or where school choice is shaped by factors other than distance.

The kriging-based accessibility measure captures the spatial distribution of school places, but it does not account for barriers in the transport network, route safety, traffic conditions, or the quality of walking infrastructure. The routing-based travel-time measure addresses this limitation more directly by using the road and path network, but it still depends on the assumed walking speed and on the completeness and accuracy of OpenStreetMap data.
Finally, the workflow could be repeated using settlement-level data as a complementary analysis. Settlement-level travel tables can describe travel behaviour for whole towns or urban areas, rather than only Census Small Areas. This may provide a broader view of how school provision and active travel relate at the town scale, and could be useful for comparing with previous work on Irish settlements. However, settlement-level data are less spatially detailed than Census Small Area data, so they would be better suited as a complementary robustness or contextual analysis rather than a replacement for the main local-scale model.


## Comparison with Previous Work
The motivation for this work came from Mancini's research on adolescent active transport in Ireland, which argued that differences in active travel between areas are linked to the geography of school provision rather than simply to population size [@mancini2025census; @mancini2024rte]. The findings here are broadly consistent with that argument, but they add a spatial dimension to it. Where Mancini focused on the presence and type of school provision, the results presented here show that even where provision appears adequate in straight-line terms, active travel can still be limited if schools are not reachable on foot through the local network.

In this sense, the present analysis complements rather than contradicts the earlier work. It supports the idea that active school travel is shaped by the geography of provision, while highlighting that the connectivity of the network is an additional and important part of that geography. The "postcode lottery" of active travel may therefore depend not only on whether school places exist nearby, but on whether the surrounding network allows children to walk to them. Working at the finer Census Small Area scale, rather than the settlement level, made it possible to detect the local severance effects that a coarser analysis would miss.

# Conclusions
The aim of this work was to examine whether school-place accessibility is associated with active school travel across Ireland, using two complementary measures: a kriging-based measure of school-place density based on straight-line distance, and a walking accessibility measure based on actual network travel time. By comparing the two measures across 16,167 Census Small Areas and modelling their association with active travel in urban areas, the analysis tested the idea that opportunities for walking and cycling to school may depend on where children live. 

The two measures agreed on average but diverged in many individual areas. These divergences consistently reflected severance, where physical barriers such as motorways, rivers, and stretches of water cut an area off from schools that are nearby in straight-line terms but not reachable on foot. The Jacob's Island Census Small Area in Cork (047132051) illustrates this clearly: it carries a kriged school-place density of 2,303 per 100 children-above the 95th percentile nationally among urban CSAs and yet its walking accessibility is exactly zero because the Mahon estuary and the South Ring Road make every nearby school unreachable within 30 minutes on foot. This pattern was not isolated: across the urban modelling sample, 82 Census Small Areas had zero walking accessibility despite above-median kriged density, of which Table 1 lists the fifteen most extreme cases, and the bivariate map showed these severance areas concentrated along the coast, on peninsulas, and around estuaries at national scale.

The statistical model reinforced this picture. The walking accessibility measure, based on network travel time along the actual road and path network, had a strong and fairly certain association with active travel: predicted active travel rose from around 15\% at the lowest levels of walking accessibility to around 60\% at the highest, with a narrow credible interval throughout. The kriging measure, based on straight-line distance, had only a small and uncertain association, with predicted active travel varying within a band of roughly 41\% to 44\% across its full range. Both models converged well, with maximum $\hat{R}$ values of 1.002 and 1.001 respectively and no divergent transitions.

Taken together, these results suggest that what matters most for active school travel is not how close schools are in straight-line terms, but whether they can actually be reached on foot. This has practical implications for how school accessibility is measured and for how active travel is supported: network-based measures capture the real opportunity for walking more faithfully than straight-line measures, and local infrastructure that overcomes barriers, pedestrian crossings, footbridges, and safe routes around estuaries and motorways perhaps are as important as the broader distribution of school places in shaping opportunities for active school travel.

This analysis focused on walking accessibility; several natural extensions follow from it. First, the travel-time measure used a step decay function with a hard 30-minute cut-off, treating all reachable school places equally regardless of travel time. Applying a continuous decay function so that more distant school places contribute less to the score, while extending the threshold to 45 minutes, would make the travel-time measure more comparable in 
catchment to the kriging measure, which captures school-place density over a wider area with an implicit decay through the variogram structure; both adjustments are supported within the r5r framework: the decay function through the \texttt{decay\_function} argument and the extended threshold through the \texttt{cutoff} parameter in \texttt{r5r::accessibility} [@pereira2021r5r]. Second, the fifteen Census Small Areas in Celbridge-Leixlip on the south-western Dublin fringe --- all carrying raw kriging values of 498--505 and sitting above the 99th percentile of the national distribution despite normal child populations and only a single nearby school point --- point to over-smoothing from the long-range Gaussian variogram fitted here; reducing the variogram range and increasing the nugget would allow local variation in dense urban-fringe areas to be better resolved. Third, separating the analysis by school level would allow primary and post-primary accessibility to be matched more precisely to the age groups each measure is intended to serve. Finally, repeating the analysis at settlement level would contextualise these Census Small Area findings within the broader town-scale patterns examined in previous Irish research on school provision and active transport [@mancini2025census].
